utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen; good afternoon to the technical booth, the interpreters, the registry staff. Madam Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is case number IT-98-29-PT, the Prosecution versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances. The Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Mark Ierace. I appear for the Prosecution, together with, on my left, Michael Blaxill, trial attorney; on my immediate right, Edel Guzman, our case manager; on my far right, Chester Stamp, who is a trial attorney replacing Sureta Chana, who has left the case; and behind me, legal officer, Stefan Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Ierace. Now the Defence, please. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good afternoon. My name is Mara Pilipovic. With my legal assistant, Mr. Savo Pilipovic, I represent the defence of General Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I am really very, very sorry for this delay. I don't have the right words to express my apologies to you. Anyway, the words are lacking. It's not really -- it is really my fault and not the fault of any other people, and I do apologise. So let us begin now. We are here in accordance with the Scheduling Order of the 21st of February, 2001. Therefore, today's hearing will be a Status Conference to analyse and see where we stand with respect to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure. We will also consider the motion of the Prosecution for travel to Sarajevo, dated the 14th of July, 2000, and perhaps I would suggest that we begin with this point, after which we will have the Status Conference proper to see how we stand with respect to the provisions of Rule 65 ter. So we come to the motion for travel to Sarajevo. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I note that on some past occasions submissions in this Chamber on that topic have been confidential. Does Your Honour wish that these proceedings this afternoon be confidential as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there may be aspects which would require that we go into private session, and this would probably be preferable even for the Defence, so let us go into private session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now we can pass on to our Status Conference. I should like to say that I have in mind a sort of general scheme for this Status Conference. We will follow the order from the Scheduling Order, but in my mind, the main objective is to take stock of the situation on the basis of the brief filed by the Prosecution, and we thank you very much for your cooperation. I also have in mind that perhaps we should have in mind during our debates the Celebici ruling and the Tadic appeals rulings as well, and if we can get any advantage from agreements or, rather, judicial notice. Also, as a major point, is the question of reciprocal communication. We know that we still haven't completed this, but we must always view things in their entirety, in the light of these three main points, if I may call them that. So before embarking upon the main issues of the Status Conference, I should like to suggest a plan of work for the months to come. So that the Chamber may supervise the preparation of the case, I suggest that the parties meet in my presence, that is, in the presence of the Pre-Trial Judge, once a month up till July in order to discuss the progress made. Each of those Status Conferences will be devoted to different issues, bearing in mind the objectives and contents of Rule 65 ter [Realtime transcript read in error "64 ter"]. Allow me to explain. But before referring to that content, I would like to say that I suggest that the parties meet in my presence each month, but there is nothing to prevent the parties from having meetings outside this courtroom and not necessarily in the presence of General Galic. Some of those working meetings could even be coordinated --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I have only one small objection about translation. Now we see that it reads "Rule 64 ter" and I heard "65 ter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. Thank you very much. We're talking about 65 ter. I'm sure the court reporters will correct that at the end. As I was saying, there is nothing to prevent the holding of working meetings amongst us, and those meetings may be coordinated by the legal officer once instructions or directives have been given for such working meetings. Let me tell you why I'm saying that. My experience tells me that it is always important for the Prosecutor and Defence counsel, that is, both counsel, should meet and discuss things together. If we limit our discussions to meetings in the courtroom, we hear each other, yes; but from the point of view of productivity, of achieving agreements, very often the progress is not as one would wish. If one goes to a certain place and meets to discuss a certain matter, achieve a certain result, and on the basis of the result, then we could say, "Have you considered this situation or this hypothesis or another situation?" and then this date and the contents that I have indicated will be a kind of turning point between previous meetings and the following meetings. It will be a kind of follow-up to things we have discussed here. As I have said, those meetings can be held outside the courtroom. They would not be formal meetings but really working meetings. What is the content which I feel needs to be organised in this way? It is always as a suggestion that I am making this to the parties. If you look at Rule 65 ter, you have paragraph (E), which tells you the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. objectives of the Pre-Trial Conference, and (ii) and (iii), which talk, in a general nature, of the Prosecution case, the matters of fact and law which are contested and those which are not in dispute, and also agreement on disagreements. I think this is very important. Why? Because it is agreement on disputed issues that will define the actual objective of the debate. Therefore, I would suggest, as a first objective of the discussion between the Prosecution and the Defence, that that should be the first point. Why am I saying this? Because we have suggested to the Prosecutor to give us the pre-trial brief, which they have done, even though it is provisional, so that they may use it as a tool, as an instrument of their work. What I think is that in order to facilitate the work of the Defence, instead of saying that we are going to discuss the whole pre-trial issue, we are going to debate and analyse this particular issue, but it is a set of issues which have a certain logic and follow logically on to each subsequent stage. Things are linked together, as you know. If we analyse well everything on which agreement has been reached, things that are contested, if we are aware of the Prosecution case and if we reach conclusions on that and disputed matters of fact and law, we are ready to go on to (iv), that is, everything that has to do with the testimony, that is, the list of witnesses the Prosecution intends to call, indicating several things. But instead of talking about a list of witnesses, we would also discuss the entire testimony, the testimony of witnesses who will come to the courtroom, the witnesses that will appear through affidavits, expert witness statements, depositions, video testimony; therefore, everything that has to do with the testimony. Instead of talking about a list of witnesses, we will be talking about the evidence which will prove the points which are in dispute. As soon as we reach conclusions on the basis of this methodology of meetings that I have suggested, we will have come to the next major topic of Rule 65 ter, that is, a list of exhibits. Again, instead of talking about a list of exhibits, I would suggest that we discuss, in a broader sense, every kind of document; for example, expert reports, disclosure of lists of exhibits. You see, there would be a logical sequence and a division of several areas which, in my view, would facilitate the life of the Prosecution, but also and above all, the work of the Defence. Why? I would like to facilitate the work of the parties and, of course, also of the Chamber and myself, so that we should be quite clear that we will be discussing the whole issue of the pre-trial stage but in segments that are linked to one another. So if we agree on a particular point of fact and law, and especially if we agree on facts, I can go on to discussing how we can prove those facts through evidence, and we will discuss that alone. And then it would be logical to address everything that has to do with the evidence, that is, the documents. So instead of analysing each of those points now, where we stand in relation to this or that, I would suggest that we begin to work together in this way that I have just described. So I leave that suggestion with you and I would like to hear your reaction. But, as I have just said, we are going to have a meeting every month but that means that we might have two meetings, for instance, before the meeting here in the courtroom, we could have informal meetings in my office or somewhere else, with the parties; the presence of General Galic is not necessary. He will be able to follow progress made because we will be coming back here in the courtroom every month. So we would have these informal meetings with the assistance of the legal officers. So, as I have just said, there is the content side, which I have divided up into three segments, and then the methodology aspect. The courtroom will be the place where we will share information about everything we have agreed upon, and even the meetings that will be held outside the courtroom will always be reported upon so that all the information would be available. So that is my suggestion and I would like to hear your reaction to these suggestions, because I have said, the objective is to reach July and have the case ready for trial by then. I have already told you that this Chamber will certainly not be opening the trial, but it is the duty of this Chamber to leave things well-prepared for whoever it will be that will be trying the case. So, Mr. Ierace, what is your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the matters of law, the provisional pre-trial brief provides an ideal vehicle for discussion between the Prosecution and Defence with a view to narrowing what the issues are in terms of the law. In relation to the evidence, might I respectfully suggest that a convenient way to approach that would be to do so by subheadings of evidence, for example, one particular monthly meeting might consider the evidence which pertains to the scheduled sniping incidents. The Defence could indicate which parts of the evidence of the sniping incidents it takes exception to, in other words, which parts it has no objection to and which parts it does, which parts it requires the Prosecution to prove by the calling of sworn evidence or the tendering of exhibits. That process, whilst it would involve considerable time on the part of the Prosecution and Defence leading up to the monthly meeting, would predictably not involve nearly as much time in the chamber and would ultimately save much time during the course of the trial. There would be, it follows, four monthly meetings or eight bi-monthly meetings between now and July, and there is a -- there is extensive evidentiary material that would have to be covered during the course of those meetings. I respectfully submit that perhaps, for the first meeting, we focus on a relatively small body of evidence because I anticipate that in that first meeting we will be refining the process of going through the evidence. Since my friend has the Pre-Trial brief, there would be no impediment to the Defence commencing its review of the statements of law which are contained within that document, that is, the provisional Pre-Trial brief. That amplifies the law which is relied upon as set out in the indictment. Perhaps each meeting could consider one aspect of the law or one section of the Pre-Trial brief which relates to statements of law, as well as a particular body of evidence. A convenient body of evidence for the first such meeting perhaps may be the remaining sniping incidents, or at least, say, ten sniping incidents. Perhaps my friend and I could agree upon ten - we are meeting tomorrow, as it is, at 2.00 - and by correspondence inform the Court which particular ten sniping incidents we propose to deal with at the first monthly meeting. That could be combined with an aspect of the law which is covered by the Pre-Trial brief. Your Honour, I offer that as merely a suggestion as to how we might proceed. And whilst that is not much in terms of what has to be covered over eight meetings, I anticipate that the process will become refined, and that will enable us to cover more of the evidentiary material in matters of law as we progress. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Ms. Pilipovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my friend just said that we are going to hold a meeting tomorrow afternoon at 2.00 p.m., and bearing in mind your points, which we accept fully, we will come up with a schedule that would incorporate your proposals. Regarding the submission on the 23rd of February, we believe that it will help the Defence prepare its case, but it is also clear that it does not contain points of fact, even though it does contain points of law. My friend also mentioned in his letter of the 14th about the difficulties that they are encountering. They are similar to the ones encountered by the Defence. I believe that tomorrow in the meeting we will come up with a plan which we will be able to then follow. I would also like to inform the Trial Chamber that pursuant to point 1 of your order ordering disclosure, the Defence has provided certain material to the OTP which my investigators were able to collect in the last month and a half. I would also like to point out that there are certain difficulties in gathering this material, because the Sarajevo Romanija Corps has been disbanded. We have information that part of that material has been destroyed, part has been lost, but the Defence will do its utmost to disclose all the material which it gathers, pursuant to Rule 66(A) and 68. Also, I received information from my friends that part of the material which is indispensable to the Defence for its further preparation I will able to receive by 6 April of this year. We expect that jointly we will be able to focus on working together, and, as we agreed today, tomorrow we will focus on facts on which we can agree and which are in dispute. This will be one of the foci of our meeting tomorrow, and I think we will use subsequent meetings to further these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly, you agree, in general terms, with this plan of work that I have suggested. Mr. Ierace, let me mention another issue. If you agree with this proposition, that is one question. And another is: I believe that you will be having a meeting tomorrow, or shortly, and you will be discussing a timetable in accordance with the instructions of the Pre-Trial Judge. So my other question is whether you would accept that the legal officers may be present with you to help with the organisational aspects and the scheduling aspects. Those are my two questions: agreement with this plan and presence of the legal officer for organisational assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do agree with the plan, and in relation to the presence of legal officers, does Your Honour have in mind legal officers of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Mr. Olivier Fourmy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic, same question to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand your proposal to mean that the legal officer should attend our meeting so that they would know about our schedule of meetings; in other words, that we would inform them on when these meetings would be held. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you were going to discuss the organisation of work, and instead of me issuing a Scheduling Order off the bat, I would prefer the parties, together with the legal officer, to draft that Scheduling Order themselves, on the basis of which we will continue to work. So the presence of the legal officer is simply to help in the organisation and execution of this work plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and that is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I must ask Mr. Olivier Fourmy whether he is available and willing. I see him nodding in the affirmative. He has no microphone to use, so that's fine. I think that having established this work plan and a schedule, I hope we will be able to reach July, once we have gone through all the stages, and we have this working tool provided by the Prosecution, so I think we can now really move on into a stage of greater effectiveness. I don't think that we have any other specific issues to raise regarding the Status Conference. Is there anything else that anyone would like to raise? Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are a few matters. Firstly, in relation to evidence by videolink, that is something which the Prosecution favours, in particular, from Sarajevo. In relation to four of the sniping incidents, which are not in question otherwise, there are witnesses in each of the four who would either prefer or who would insist upon giving videolink evidence, in other words, not travelling to The Hague. The reasons for that range from age - one witness is aged 81 - to family reasons and to health. If it is acceptable to the Chamber, I have in mind that those witnesses, and perhaps others, could give their evidence from within the United Nations field office in Sarajevo so that they could be examined and cross-examined and shown exhibits by videolink from the Trial Chamber here at The Hague. Your Honour, there is one remaining matter. There have been some discussions between my friend and I in relation to an order of the Chamber dated the 5th of June last year. In that order, the Chamber established a protocol to apply when one party wishes to question either a witness or potential witness of the other party. It appears at paragraph 7 of the orders made on that date. Effectively, it requires the interviewing party to contact the other party, given in writing and allowing reasonable notice. It also requires that if the witness to be interviewed so requests, then the party who intends to call that witness may be present at any such meetings. Your Honour, many of the individuals whose identity has been disclosed from one side to the other clearly fall into the category of being a witness or potential witness, but beyond those two categories there are many names which are not so easily categorised. My friend and I are content at this stage to attempt to resolve that issue between ourselves and in due course inform the Chamber of the result of those discussions so that there is a public record of it. However, if we are unable to resolve it, if it is a matter which requires an order of the Court, then so be it, and we would seek leave to approach the Chamber on short notice to have that issue resolved, because if it is not, it will impede the investigations by both the Prosecution and the Defence. It does need quick resolution. We are hopeful that we can resolve that tomorrow afternoon. If not, would Your Honour allow us to contact the Chamber to seek an early hearing date of that issue? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite, Mr. Ierace. We are quite ready to hear your submissions, if necessary. Perhaps, Ms. Pilipovic, you can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. My friend and I have agreed that tomorrow we will attempt to meet and find a position that is jointly acceptable. I would like to take the opportunity and raise the question of the experts whom the Defence would try to call. We approached the registry with the request: a ballistic expert for shelling, an expert for sniping, a military expert, and a historian. The Defence estimates that the amount of time needed for these experts to produce their findings, taking into account the scope of this case and the time frame, this time frame would in total be about 520 hours for all experts involved. However, we have not received a decision on the part of the registry so far, but we need to proceed with our preparations, and we would seek assistance from the Trial Chamber to help us speed up this process of decision-making on this issue. The second issue that I wanted to raise has to do with your decision of the 5th of June, page 3, paragraph 4, regarding disclosure of material and confidential information which the Defence would provide to the experts. We would like to ask whether we need special authority by the Trial Chamber to turn over these confidential materials in our possession to the experts, the experts that the Defence is seeking to call on behalf of General Galic. These are the issues which I have raised, and perhaps I can also expect your response in writing or perhaps also in another Status Conference. However, it would be in the interests of the Defence to receive such ruling in writing, preferably. Also, I would like to ask about the decision on our cameramen which would be coming with us to the Sarajevo trip. The issue is the fact that they may have some problems in going to Sarajevo. I don't know what the effect would be of the presence of the Defence with their own camera crew in the city of Sarajevo. Perhaps we may need your assistance in that. Should we turn to the registry for this? Or perhaps the Trial Chamber can go to the registry itself so that we get the permission to have our own crew film all the locations mentioned in the indictment so that my friends from the Prosecution and myself could have this material developed in time for the trial and so that we could adequately prepare for the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. I don't know whether Mr. Ierace has any reaction or comments to make on matters raised by Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists Ms. Pilipovic in her dealings with the registry, and indeed if it assists Your Honour, the Prosecution does intend to call experts in the area of ballistics. Indeed, we intend to call an expert or experts in relation to artillery, as well as the capability of small arms such as rifles and machine-guns. That may be of some assistance to my friend in terms of arguing to the Registry that there is a prima facie entitlement to respond to our expert evidence. We do not intend to call an historian so I can't assist her with that. In relation to the application of the orders of the 5th of June last year to the provision of information to an expert, my friend referred to paragraph 4 of the orders. I think that paragraph 4 is confined to nonpublic information, that is, information which has come into the possession of the Defence from the Prosecution which is then deemed to be of a confidential nature. I have difficulty in imagining what such information would be relevant or useful to an expert, certainly a ballistics expert or an historian. Your Honour, in relation to the third point raised by my friend, that is, securing ease of access to Sarajevo, naturally, it is in the interests of justice in this trial that both sides have equal access to all relevant sites in Sarajevo, and the Prosecution acknowledges that proposition. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Ierace. I think we have several points here that we need to clarify further to be able to work on them. But I think there are also aspects which can be an object of discussion at our next meeting. The question of video testimony, we can develop that when we come to the question of testimony in general. But, of course, there are things that can be prepared in advance. The question of expert witnesses, Ms. Pilipovic, this is a problem that you should resolve with the Registry. If you are not satisfied with the decision of the Registry, then you must address the President of the Tribunal, because the Chamber does not have any powers over the Registry. This may be strange for people from the civil law system, but that is how it is. The administrative powers are held by the President of the Tribunal. If you ask the Registry for something and it does not respond in the way you expected it to, you have to address yourself to the President of the Tribunal. So I think that is all we can do today. I believe you will be meeting tomorrow to discuss logistical and practical matters. You will tell Mr. Fourmy where and when you will meet so he can join you regarding the schedule, and after that we can prepare a series of questions which we can develop jointly. I think that a summary that we can make of what we have done today would be that we have at least identified more or less structured contents and more or less structured methodology which together can help us to make progress in preparing the case. I think there is also a novel element and that is the presence of the legal officer of the Chamber as an element in between the Trial Chamber and the parties, and I think this can be an asset which can contribute to further progress. Before adjourning, I would like to address General Galic. General Galic, can you stand, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to ask you what you know I'm going to ask you, because that is part of our Rules, to ask you how things are, how you are feeling, and how your conditions of detention are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to thank you for asking these questions. I have nothing special to say. Now the Status Conferences are frequent enough and not so much changes during that period in the Detention Unit. But thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General Galic. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So tomorrow I can say that we will be meeting, though indirectly, and further progress will be made. I really hope that some important results will be achieved for our next Status Conference, that there will be some good agreements and some good disagreements; that is, we will be able to identify clearly the things that divide us and the points that we have in common so that the case can be well-prepared when the time comes. I wish you success in your work tomorrow, and until our next meeting, this hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
